teacher: T5-XL (~3B params) supervised fine-tuned on each task; for GSM8K, Flan-T5-XL fine-tuned on PaLM-540B-generated CoT data (accuracy 27.9); for task-agnostic distillation, Flan-T5-XL.
student: T5-Small (77M), T5-Base (250M), T5-Large (800M) — all starting from LM-adapted T5v1.1 checkpoints supervised fine-tuned on respective tasks; for GSM8K, Flan-T5 variants fine-tuned for 10K steps on CoT data. Capacity ratios: 38×, 12×, 3.8× smaller than teacher respectively.
rationale: T5 model family chosen to systematically study distillation across different student-teacher capacity ratios (38×, 12×, 3.8×) using the same pretrained architecture. Open-sourced T5 models enable reproducibility.
training_data: XSum (news summarization dataset), WMT14 en-de (machine translation), GSM8K (~5.3K problem-CoT pairs from PaLM-540B-generated CoTs by Magister et al.), FLAN2021 (for task-agnostic instruction tuning).
loss_details: Token-level divergence D(pT || pS) averaged over sequence length. Divergences explored: Forward KL, Reverse KL, JSD(0.1), JSD(0.5), JSD(0.9). Student data fraction λ ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}. On-policy (λ=1) uses student-generated outputs; no gradient through sampling. Best divergence is task-dependent: Forward KL for XSum (greedy) and GSM8K; JSD(0.1) for WMT; Reverse KL for task-agnostic distillation. Teacher softmax temperature: 1.0 for WMT and instruction tuning; 0.1 for XSum (temp sampling eval) and GSM8K. Student training temperature γ=1.
task: XSum abstractive summarization (ROUGE-2), WMT14 en-de translation (BLEU with beam search), GSM8K arithmetic reasoning with 4-shot CoT (accuracy with calculator), task-agnostic instruction tuning evaluated on BBH (23 tasks) and MMLU (57 tasks) few-shot accuracy.
notes: On-policy GKD showed the largest relative gains on summarization (2.1× over baselines), followed by arithmetic reasoning (1.9×) and translation (1.7×). The optimal divergence is task-dependent: forward KL works well with greedy decoding, while mode-seeking divergences (reverse KL, JSD(0.9)) excel with temperature sampling by avoiding low-quality generations. On-policy data consistently outperformed fixed supervised data across all tasks, and GKD combined with RL fine-tuning (RLEF) substantially improved factual consistency on summarization beyond what the teacher achieves.

teacher: Same-size setting: Qwen3-4B-Non-Thinking-RL-Math and Qwen3-4B-Non-Thinking-RL-Code (domain-specific RL variants of the student). Strong-to-weak setting: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Reward correction experiments: Qwen3-4B-Non-Thinking-RL-Math/Code as teachers.
student: Same-size setting: Qwen3-4B-Non-Thinking. Strong-to-weak setting: Qwen3-1.7B-Non-Thinking and Qwen3-4B-Non-Thinking.
rationale: Same-size pairs test multi-teacher merging of domain-specific RL experts back into the original base model. Strong-to-weak pairs (30B-A3B → 1.7B/4B) test distilling a larger teacher into a smaller student. Reward correction experiments use 4B→1.7B to test when teacher's pre-RL variant is available.
training_data: Math: 57K samples filtered from DeepMath (difficulty ≥ 6). Code: 25K samples from Eurus-RL-Code. Distillation data is the same as the RL data.
loss_details: G-OPD objective: max E[λ · log(π*/π_ref) - D_KL(π_θ || π_ref)]. Standard OPD corresponds to λ=1.0 (reverse KL divergence on student-generated trajectories). ExOPD uses λ=1.25 (reward extrapolation). Explored λ ∈ {0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5}. Reference model π_ref is the student base model by default; reward correction sets π_ref to teacher's pre-RL variant. Discount factor of 0 (next-token optimization only). No explicit temperature parameter; β=1 implicitly.
task: Math reasoning: AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25 (February), HMMT25 (November). Code generation: HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench (v6, Feb 2025–May 2025). Evaluation: temperature=1.0, top-p=1.0, max generation length=16384, 32 samples per math problem, 4 samples per code problem.
notes: ExOPD (λ=1.25) consistently outperforms standard OPD (λ=1.0) across all settings. In multi-teacher distillation, ExOPD is the only method that produces a unified student surpassing all domain teachers (avg math 47.7 vs teacher 46.0, avg code 62.0 vs teacher 61.2). In strong-to-weak distillation (30B→1.7B/4B), ExOPD shows large gains over OPD (e.g., 45.3 vs 35.1 avg math for 4B student). Excessive extrapolation (λ=1.5) can degrade performance due to reward hacking. Reward correction (using teacher's pre-RL base as reference) further boosts ExOPD but requires access to an additional model and incurs higher compute.

teacher: GPT-2 XL (1.5B), OpenLLaMA2-7B, T5-XL v1.1 (3B), mT5-XL. Multiple teacher-student pairs evaluated.
student: GPT-2 (0.1B/124M), GPT-2 Large, OpenLLaMA2-3B (with LoRA rank 16), T5-Base (0.2B), T5-Small (0.06B), mT5-Base, mT5-Small.
rationale: Follows experimental setup of MiniLLM (Gu et al., 2024) for fair comparison. Capacity ratios range from ~15x (GPT-2 XL→GPT-2) to ~2.3x (OpenLLaMA2-7B→3B). Multiple pairs used to demonstrate generalizability across model scales.
training_data: databricks-dolly-15k (14K training, 500 validation, 500 test) for instruction-following; OpenWebText corpus for language modeling loss; SAMSum (16K conversations) for summarization; XSum (20K random samples used); CNN/DM (20K random samples used); IWSLT 2017 En-De (full dataset) for machine translation.
loss_details: Skew Reverse KL divergence (SRKL) with α=0.1 as default. D_SKL^(α)(p, q_θ) = D_KL(p, αp + (1-α)q_θ). Combined with adaptive off-policy approach using initial probability ϕ=0, replay buffer size 1000, linearly decreasing replay ratio λ_R = ϕ(1-t/T). Language modeling loss on OpenWebText added for instruction-following experiments. No explicit temperature parameter mentioned (implicit τ=1.0).
task: Task-agnostic instruction-following (Dolly Eval, Self-Instruct, Vicuna Eval, Super-Natural Instructions, Unnatural Instructions), text summarization (SAMSum, XSum, CNN/DM), machine translation (IWSLT 2017 En-De). Metrics: ROUGE-L, BLEU, GPT-4 feedback.
notes: DistiLLM achieves 2.5–4.3× training speedup over MiniLLM and GKD while achieving state-of-the-art ROUGE-L scores. The biggest improvements are on task-agnostic instruction-following benchmarks (e.g., Super-Natural and Unnatural Instructions), where SRKL with adaptive off-policy achieves 28.24 and 30.11 ROUGE-L respectively for GPT-2 XL→GPT-2. Performance margins are smaller on single-task scenarios (summarization/translation), and the method shows that effectiveness of SGO and loss functions is task-dependent, but DistiLLM's adaptive scheduler consistently outperforms manual tuning across tasks.

teacher: GPT2-1.5B (for GPT2-120M student), LLaMA2-7B (for TinyLLaMA-1.1B student), OLMo2-7B (for OLMo2-1B), Qwen2.5-1.5B (for Qwen2.5-0.5B), Gemma3-4B (for Gemma3-1B)
student: GPT2-120M (full fine-tuning), TinyLLaMA-1.1B (LoRA), OLMo2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Gemma3-1B
rationale: Multiple teacher-student pairs chosen to demonstrate generalizability across diverse model families and scales. Capacity ratios include 12.5x (GPT2-1.5B→120M), ~6.4x (LLaMA2-7B→TinyLLaMA-1.1B), 7x (OLMo2-7B→1B), 3x (Qwen2.5-1.5B→0.5B), and 4x (Gemma3-4B→1B).
training_data: databricks/dolly-15k dataset: 11K training samples, 1K validation samples, 500 test samples.
loss_details: Token-wise adaptive combination of Forward KL and Reverse KL: L_ToDi = α_{t,i} · D_FKL^{(t,i)} + (1 - α_{t,i}) · D_RKL^{(t,i)}, where α_{t,i} = sg[σ(β · log(p/q_θ))] with β=1 (default sigmoid), stop-gradient on the weight. Training loss = 0.5 × KD loss + 0.5 × cross-entropy loss. No temperature parameter mentioned (implicit τ=1).
task: Instruction-following benchmarks: DollyEval (500 examples), S-NI (1,694 examples), UnNI (10,000 examples), SelfInst (242 examples), VicunaEval (80 examples). Evaluated with ROUGE-L metric and GPT-4 pairwise preference evaluation (gpt-4o-2024-11-20).
notes: ToDi achieved the highest average ROUGE-L across all five instruction-following benchmarks for both GPT2 and TinyLLaMA settings, with the largest gains on S-NI (19.42 vs. next-best 18.60 for GPT2) and DollyEval (26.26 vs. 25.50 for TinyLLaMA). The method maintains O(V) linear time complexity (vs. O(V log V) for AKL) and shows stable convergence. The default β=1 outperforms all other β values; reversed weighting (β=-1) degrades performance, confirming the importance of the theoretically-motivated direction of the adaptive weighting.

teacher: GPT-2 1.5B and LLaMA 6.7B (both fine-tuned on the instruction-response dataset before distillation)
student: GPT-2 120M and TinyLLaMA 1.1B
rationale: Capacity ratios are approximately 12.5x (GPT-2 1.5B→120M) and ~6x (LLaMA 6.7B→TinyLLaMA 1.1B). These pairs were chosen following the setup of Gu et al. (2023) to demonstrate KD for LLMs at different scales.
training_data: Instruction-response dataset built from databricks-dolly-15k: 14k training samples, 500 validation samples, 500 test samples.
loss_details: AKL = (g_head/(g_head+g_tail)) * FKL + (g_tail/(g_head+g_tail)) * RKL, where g_head and g_tail are computed as the sum of pointwise absolute differences |p(Yi)-q(Yi)| over head and tail tokens respectively. Head/tail split determined by threshold µ=0.5 (tokens sorted by teacher probability until cumulative mass ≥ µ). No temperature mentioned (implicit τ=1.0). Gap function ε(p(z),q(z))=|p(z)-q(z)|. No NLL mixing term mentioned.
task: Dolly (500 samples), S-NI (1694 samples), UnNI (10000 samples) evaluated via Rouge-L scores over 5 seeds. Also evaluated on Winogrande (zero-shot), OpenBookQA (zero-shot), BoolQ (zero-shot), ARC challenge (5-shot). GPT-4-based diversity and quality scoring. Human evaluation (win/tie/loss).
notes: AKL showed the biggest improvements on the larger UnNI dataset (21.97 vs 20.37 for FKL+RKL on GPT-2; 31.05 vs 30.48 on TinyLLaMA), with p-values < 0.001 against FKL+RKL. It also consistently outperformed all baselines on additional benchmarks (Winogrande, OpenBookQA, BoolQ, ARC). GPT-4 evaluations confirmed AKL improves both diversity (5.63 vs 5.51 for FKL+RKL) and quality (5.72 vs 5.36) of generated responses. The method adds modest overhead (~40.3G GPU memory vs 37.5G for FKL+RKL).

teacher: Qwen2.5-7B (pretrained) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (finetuned). Teacher evaluation uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
student: Qwen2.5-1.5B (pretrained base model, initialized as πsraw). Authors mention LLaMA-3 family as future work but only present Qwen2.5 results.
rationale: 7B teacher vs 1.5B student (~4.7x capacity ratio). Chosen because the representational capacities of large and small models are fundamentally different, motivating the need to transfer the behavioral shift (delta) rather than absolute outputs. The paper argues that directly matching a 7B teacher's distribution is unreachable for a 1.5B student.
training_data: ultrachat-200k (instruction tuning) and OpenMathReasoning (reasoning). Authors note they sampled small subsets of the original datasets to reduce training time; exact subset sizes are not specified.
loss_details: L_total = λ * L_SFT + (1 - λ) * L_delta-KD, where L_delta-KD = D_KL(πs* || πθ). The synthetic target πs*(yt|x) = (1/Z) * πt_ft(yt|x) * (πs_raw(yt|x) / πt_raw(yt|x))^α, with Z as a token-level partition function for normalization. α ∈ [0,1] controls intensity of behavioral shift alignment. Temperature-scaled softmax with parameter τ is applied to logits. Exact values of λ, α, and τ are not explicitly reported.
task: Instruction following (ultrachat-200k) and mathematical reasoning (OpenMathReasoning), evaluated using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L on non-overlapping test splits.
notes: Delta-KD consistently outperforms all baselines (SFT, FKL, RKL, SeqKD, MiniLLM) on both benchmarks. The largest improvements appear on OpenMathReasoning ROUGE-2 (0.2664 vs. 0.2389 for next-best SeqKD, +0.0275 absolute) and Ultrachat ROUGE-1 (0.5407 vs. 0.5211 for MiniLLM, +0.0196). The paper is marked as work in progress—exact hyperparameter values (λ, α, τ), dataset subset sizes, and LLM-based evaluation are deferred to future work, and results on LLaMA-3 models are not yet provided.

teacher: Qwen3-8B (non-thinking mode) for Qwen3 students; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for Llama students.
student: Qwen3-0.6B-Base, Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Qwen3-4B-Base; additionally Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.
rationale: Qwen3-8B serves as a same-family teacher for three progressively larger Qwen3-Base students (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B), enabling analysis of scaling effects. Llama experiments verify generality across architectures. Capacity ratios range from ~13× (8B/0.6B) to ~2× (8B/4B).
training_data: MATH dataset for Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base; DAPO-Math-14k for Qwen3-4B-Base. Exact sample counts for MATH not explicitly stated; DAPO-Math-14k implies 14k samples.
loss_details: Dynamically switches between reverse KL (clipped PPO-style surrogate with clip ε) at low teacher-entropy tokens and forward KL (top-k=16 truncated) at high teacher-entropy tokens (entropy threshold τ=0.8). Reverse KL uses per-token advantage Ât = log πte(xt|ct) − log πθ_old(xt|ct) with PPO clipping. Forward KL is approximated over teacher's top-16 tokens. No explicit temperature scaling (training temperature=1.0). Off-policy KD baseline uses CE loss weight 0.5 + KL loss weight 0.5.
task: Six math reasoning benchmarks: MATH500, AMC23, Minerva, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AIME25. Out-of-domain: GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AlpacaEval 2.0. Metrics: Avg@8 and Pass@8.
notes: EOPD shows the largest gains on harder benchmarks and larger students: Qwen3-4B-Base achieves +5.05 Pass@8 improvement over OPD averaged across six math benchmarks, with particularly strong gains on AIME24 (+10 Pass@8) and AIME25 (+3.33 Pass@8). The Pass@k gap widens as k increases, indicating better diversity preservation. The method is relatively insensitive to the entropy threshold τ (best at 0.8), and entropy-aware token selection outperforms both random and full forward KL placement, confirming that targeted forward KL at high-entropy positions is key.

teacher: Qwen2-7B and OpenLLaMA2-7B (used as teacher models for their respective distillation pairs).
student: Qwen2-1.5B and OpenLLaMA2-3B (distilled from their respective 7B teachers). LoRA with rank 16 used for parameter-efficient distillation on Qwen2 and OpenLLaMA2.
rationale: Follows the widely-adopted setup from Gu et al. and Ko et al. Qwen2-7B→1.5B (~4.7x capacity ratio) and OpenLLaMA2-7B→3B (~2.3x capacity ratio) chosen to demonstrate generalizability across two modern model families.
training_data: databricks-dolly-15k dataset (15k samples) used for training.
loss_details: Plug-and-play framework applied on top of various base losses (FKD, RKD, ABKD, GKD, DistiLLM). Token difficulty measured via Hellinger distance (Eq. 3). LATF module dynamically adjusts token selection ratio r via EMA-based feedback loop (β=0.97, ϵ=0.05, δ=0.05, warm-up ratio=0.05). IDTS assigns per-token temperature: τ_i = τ_base · exp(−c · ŝ_i) where c=0.5 (optimal), ŝ_i = tanh(log(s_i / median(s))). Low temperature for hard tokens, high temperature for easy tokens. Loss computed only on top-r% hardest tokens with τ² scaling factor in KL divergence.
task: Five instruction-following benchmarks: Dolly-eval, Self-Instruct, Vicuna-eval, Super-Natural Instructions (S-NI), and Unnatural Instructions (UnNI). Evaluated using ROUGE-L scores and LLM-as-a-Judge (Qwen3-32B) pairwise comparisons.
notes: AdaKD showed the largest improvements on the UnNI benchmark (e.g., RKD+AdaKD: 43.17 vs 39.90 baseline, +3.27 ROUGE-L) and S-NI (43.82 vs 41.68, +2.14), demonstrating strongest gains on large-scale challenging benchmarks. The IDTS module alone provides substantial gains while LATF alone yields no improvement, but their combination is synergistic—LATF removes noisy easy tokens enabling IDTS to work more effectively. The framework showed marginal improvement for FKD due to a conceptual conflict between FKD's mean-seeking objective and IDTS's targeted correction for hard tokens, as confirmed by LLM-as-a-Judge where FKD+AdaKD had more losses than wins on S-NI (26.33% loss vs 19.42% win).

teacher: GPT-2-1.5B, OpenLLaMA-7B, GEMMA-7B-IT (larger variants or self, used as teachers)
student: 未明确
loss: Concrete Score Distillation (discrete score-matching objective matching relative logit differences)
task: Task-agnostic instruction-following, task-specific distillation
notes: Resolves softmax smoothing and logit shift invariance issues; provides both mode-seeking and mode-covering variants; complementary with on-policy techniques. ICLR 2026.

teacher: GPT-2-1.5B, GPT-J 6B, OPT-13B, LLaMA-13B
student: GPT-2 120M/340M/760M, OPT 1.3B/2.7B/6.7B, LLaMA 7B
loss: Reverse KL divergence (KL[q_θ||p]) with on-policy optimization via policy gradient, single-step decomposition, teacher-mixed sampling, and length normalization
task: DollyEval, SelfInst, VicunaEval, S-NI (Super-NaturalInstructions), UnNI (Unnatural Instructions), SST2, BoolQ
notes: On-policy distillation approach for generative LLMs. Uses teacher-mixed sampling (α=0.2) to alleviate reward hacking. Includes language modeling loss on pre-training corpus to preserve canonical NLP benchmark performance. Evaluated with Rouge-L, GPT-4 feedback scores, and human evaluation. Scalable from 120M to 13B parameters across GPT-2, OPT, and LLaMA model families.

teacher: Qwen2.5-7B-Math-Instruct (Setting 1) and Llama-3.2-11B-Instruct (Setting 2)
student: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Math (Setting 1) and Llama-3.2-3B (Setting 2)
rationale: Teacher-student pairs chosen to evaluate distillation in resource-constrained settings for mathematical reasoning. Capacity ratios are approximately 4.7x (7B→1.5B) and 3.7x (11B→3B).
training_data: GSM8K training dataset (Setting 1, Qwen) and MATH training dataset (Setting 2, Llama). Exact data sizes not explicitly stated.
loss_details: Constrained reward function R̂_{π,n} that gives task reward R(s_T, a_T) when cumulative KL budget d is satisfied (d - Σ C_π(s_t) ≥ 0), and penalty -(n + φ_π(s_T)) otherwise, where φ_π is KL divergence between student and teacher at s_T and n ≫ R_max. Constraint threshold d=0.35. Optimized via GRPO policy gradient with learning rate 1e-5, AdamW optimizer, batch size 64 (8 questions × 8 answers per question). Gradient includes likelihood-ratio term plus explicit-dependence term with tolerance ε↓0 near feasibility boundary. Training runs for 20 epochs.
task: Mathematical reasoning: evaluated on Apple/GSM-Symbolic (main), GSM8K test set, and MATH full test set. Metrics: Final Answer Correctness (FAC), Reasoning Win Rate (RWR) and Reasoning Loss Rate (RLR) via LLM-as-Judge (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B), Constraint Satisfaction rate, and KL divergence.
notes: The method achieves the best balance across all evaluation dimensions: it attains the highest constraint satisfaction rates (e.g., 96.1% for Qwen on GSM-Symbolic, 94.64% for Llama) and dramatically superior reasoning win rates (e.g., 60.55% RWR on Qwen/GSM-Symbolic vs. 14.89% for pure GRPO) while maintaining competitive final answer correctness. Pure reward optimization (GRPO λ=0) achieves highest FAC but with severely degraded reasoning quality and constraint violations, while pure KL methods (GKD, Mini-LLM) satisfy constraints but underperform on FAC. The method particularly excels at reasoning quality over Lagrangian relaxation baselines (GKD-GRPO) across all λ settings.

teacher: Qwen3-8B (on-policy teacher for OPD); QwQ-32B off-policy responses from OpenThoughts3 used for SeqKD baseline.
student: Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base
rationale: Qwen3-8B serves as the on-policy teacher scoring student rollouts at token level; Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base are chosen to test prefix OPD across different capacity ratios (roughly 4.7× and 1× parameter ratio to teacher). The same-size student (8B-Base distilled from 8B-Instruct) tests whether prefix distillation works even without a capacity gap.
training_data: 30.7k questions randomly sampled from OpenThoughts3 for OPD training; 192k data for SeqKD baseline to reach comparable FLOP.
loss_details: Reverse KL divergence KL(πs ∥ πT) estimated via sampling (Eq. 1) with N=4 samples per prompt. Token-level log-ratio losses are summed over the sequence length. No temperature parameter mentioned (implicit τ=1.0). No mixture with forward KL or NLL — pure reverse KL only. Importance sampling correction applied for floating-point non-associativity during vLLM rollouts. No entropy loss or KL regularization to old policy used.
task: In-domain: MATH-500, AIME-24, AIME-25. Out-of-domain: MMLU-Pro, GPQA. Evaluation metric: Mean Acc.@16 (16 samples).
notes: Fast OPD (prefix OPD with scheduling) matches full OPD performance while reducing training FLOP by 2×–47×. The biggest efficiency gains come with short prefixes (e.g., 256 tokens at 10 steps yields 47× FLOP reduction on Qwen3-8B-Base with comparable AIME-24 accuracy). However, for the smaller Qwen3-1.7B-Base student, prefix-only training can hurt out-of-domain generalization and tail-token quality, making prefix scheduling (Ltrain starting at 1, ΔL=256 per step) essential for robust performance. Off-policy prefix distillation (prefix SeqKD) does not transfer the benefits — it quickly degrades student performance, confirming that the on-policy property is critical for prefix truncation to work.

teacher: GPT-2 XL (1.5B params), OPT-13B, Llama-13B. Teachers are supervised fine-tuned on Dolly training set before distillation. Soft prompts (7 tokens, ~11K parameters, 0.0007% of teacher params) are prepended to teacher input and tuned with student guidance.
student: GPT-2 Base (120M), GPT-2 Medium (340M), GPT-2 Large (760M); OPT-1.3B, OPT-2.7B, OPT-6.7B; Llama-7B. Students are initialized from SFT checkpoint (fine-tuned for 3 epochs on Dolly).
rationale: Capacity gap between teacher and student persists in KD for generative LMs; larger teachers do not necessarily improve student performance. Student-friendly knowledge distillation addresses this gap. Capacity ratios range from ~2x (Llama-13B→7B) to ~12.5x (GPT-2 XL→Base) and ~10x (OPT-13B→1.3B).
training_data: Dolly dataset: 15,000 human-written instruction-response pairs split into 14,000 training, 500 validation, 500 testing. Evaluation on 5 datasets: Dolly, SelfInst, Vicuna (80 questions), S-NI (Super-NaturalInstructions test set), UnNI (Unnatural Instructions). For S-NI and UnNI, only samples with ground truth response length ≥11 tokens are used.
loss_details: Prompt loss: Lprompt = Lkd + ((K-k)/K) * Lreg, where Lkd = DKL(p(y|P,x) || qθ(y|x)) (forward KL for prompt tuning), Lreg = DKL(p(y|P,x) || p(y|x)) with linearly decaying coefficient from 1 to 0 over training. Student loss: Lstudent = DKL(qθ(y|x) || p(y|P,x)) (reverse KL divergence). Pseudo-targets are student-generated responses (no backprop during sampling). Temperature fixed at 1.0.
task: Instruction-following evaluation on 5 datasets (Dolly, SelfInst, Vicuna, S-NI, UnNI) using ROUGE-L metric averaged over 5 random seeds. Also GPT-4 feedback scores measured separately.
notes: PromptKD achieves state-of-the-art performance across all model families (GPT-2, OPT, Llama) and sizes, consistently surpassing teacher performance on all 5 datasets—a feat no other baseline achieves. The method is particularly effective on out-of-distribution evaluation sets (SelfInst, Vicuna, S-NI, UnNI), demonstrating strong generalization. Analysis reveals that student-friendly knowledge effectively alleviates exposure bias throughout training, and the approach adds only ~11K trainable prompt parameters (0.0007% of teacher), making it far more efficient than MiniLLM which requires ~2x more memory and ~3x more training time.

teacher: Distillation track: Qwen3-14B (frozen). Self-distillation track: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct (frozen copy of itself). External expert for reference solution generation: gpt-oss-120b (OpenAI).
student: Distillation track: Qwen3-8B. Self-distillation track: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct (trainable copy).
rationale: Distillation uses a larger same-family teacher (14B→8B, ~1.75x capacity ratio) with forward KL for broad mode coverage when capacity differs. Self-distillation uses the same model as both teacher and student with reverse KL for compact, high-confidence mode consolidation when teacher and student are near-policy.
training_data: DAPO dataset (Yu et al., 2025), split into two disjoint partitions: one for distillation (Ddist) and one for self-distillation (Dself) to avoid cross-setting leakage. Exact data sizes not explicitly stated.
loss_details: Distillation track: Forward KL weighted by Beta kernel w(p) = p^α(1−p)^β, default α=β=1 giving w(p)=p(1−p). Self-distillation track: Reverse KL weighted by same Beta kernel. Final loss: L(θ;x) = w(p) · L_distill(θ; y_T, x). Weights normalized to unit mean (w̃_i = w_i/w̄) and kept fixed during training. Two-stage synergy: forward KL then reverse KL with 50/50 step split and pass rates recomputed once between stages. No explicit temperature parameter mentioned for KL.
task: Plasticity: mean@8 accuracy on MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025 (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 8 sampled responses). Stability: MMLU (forgetting measured as Δ from base).
notes: PACED shows largest improvements on the hardest OOD benchmarks: +14.8 on AIME 2025 (distillation) and +13.6 on AIME 2025 (self-distillation) over base models, while maintaining near-zero MMLU forgetting (0.2% and 0.6% respectively). The two-stage KL→RevKL schedule yields the strongest overall results (+9.1/+15.2/+16.7 on MATH-500/AIME24/AIME25), confirming mode-coverage-then-consolidation is superior to the reverse order, which actually underperforms both single-loss baselines. PACED consistently outperforms the token-level AKL baseline across all benchmarks, suggesting problem-level weighting by pass rate is more effective than token-level KL modulation.

teacher: SFTed Qwen-2.5-3B, SFTed Llama-3.1-3B, and SFTed Gemma-7B (teacher models are first fine-tuned on each task before distillation)
student: Qwen-2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.1-1B, and Gemma-2B
rationale: Following prior KD work (GKD, SWITCH, SKD) in selecting comparable teacher–student model scales within the same LLM family. Capacity ratios: Llama 3B→1B (3×), Qwen 3B→0.5B (6×), Gemma 7B→2B (3.5×).
training_data: DialogSum (12.5K training samples; 1K randomly sampled for KD, 1.5K test), GSM8K (7K training for teacher SFT, 473 validation; 1K randomly sampled for KD, 1.3K test), GSM-Plus (adversarial test set used for evaluation only; student models distilled on GSM8K are evaluated on GSM-Plus).
loss_details: Token-level KL divergence D(Mt || Ms) averaged over sequence length, minimized via gradient descent. Also evaluated with Reverse KL and JSD as distance metrics. Student sampling: temperature=0.5, top-p=0.5; Teacher sampling: temperature=0.2, top-p=0.5. AdaSwitch hyperparameters: sliding window length L=10, divergence threshold multiplier K=3. Adaptive threshold τ = K · d̄_{i-1} where d̄ is the sliding window moving average of KL divergences.
task: Dialogue summarization (DialogSum, evaluated with ROUGE-L), arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K, evaluated with accuracy), and robustness evaluation (GSM-Plus, evaluated with accuracy).
notes: AdaSwitch showed the biggest improvements on arithmetic reasoning tasks: on GSM8K it surpassed the second-best method by 7.2% (Llama) and 11.8% (Qwen), and achieved consistent gains on GSM-Plus for generalization. The method is robust across all three LLM families and compatible with different divergence metrics (KL, Reverse KL, JSD). Its one-time switching mechanism avoids the 'chimera' fragmentation problem of frequent-switching methods like SKD and SWITCH, with only 1.3× overhead versus pure on-policy KD (10% less than SKD/SWITCH). Performance was relatively less sensitive to hyperparameters on the easier SUMM task but more sensitive on GSM, especially for Llama.

teacher: White-box: T5-large (780M) as primary teacher, T5-base and T5-xl also used in scalability studies. Black-box: Llama-2-7b (4-bit quantized) as teacher.
student: White-box: T5-small (77M) and T5-base (250M) as primary students; T5-large used in scalability and self-distillation experiments. Black-box: T5-large (780M) as student.
rationale: T5 model family chosen for systematic size variation; primary capacity ratios are ~10:1 (780M→77M) and ~3:1 (780M→250M). Llama-2-7b used as black-box teacher to demonstrate cross-architecture and black-box applicability.
training_data: XSum (abstractive summarization, full training set, eval on validation split), WMT14 en-de (top 10k training data, eval on validation split), GSM8k (arithmetic reasoning, eval on test split). Data efficiency studies use 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of training sets. Black-box: first 1000 samples per dataset with 10 teacher-generated answers each.
loss_details: X-KD loss = base KD loss + experiential regularization (Lex). Experiential weight λ=0.001 across all variants. Boltzmann temperature τ'=1.0. Discount factor γ=1.0. Reward prior p(R) is Gaussian. For G-XKD (generalized): GKD loss uses β-JS divergence with β=0.5, on-policy weight α=0.5, plus Lex. For S-XKD (supervised): forward-KL divergence plus Lex. For SeqXKD (sequence-level): sequence-level NLL on teacher-generated samples (sampling temperature=1.0, top-p=0.95) plus Lex. Setting λ=0 recovers non-experiential baselines.
task: Abstractive summarization (XSum, ROUGE scores), machine translation (WMT14 en-de, BLEU scores), arithmetic reasoning (GSM8k, accuracy). Also: performance-diversity trade-off (SelfBLEU), data efficiency, scalability, self-distillation, and GPT-4 win-rate evaluation for black-box distillation.
notes: G-XKD consistently outperforms GKD and MiniLLM across all three tasks and both model size configurations (large→small and large→base), with the largest gains on XSum summarization (e.g., 13.81 vs 13.62 ROUGE-2 for large→small). X-KD shows strong data efficiency, achieving baseline-comparable performance with less training data, and better performance-diversity trade-offs. A key limitation is sensitivity to the experiential weight λ, with performance peaking at λ=0.001 and degrading at higher values, suggesting need for normalization techniques.

teacher: Multiple teachers used across experiments: Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct (3.8B), GPT-2 variants, Pythia variants, and larger models for TAID-LLM-1.5B and TAID-VLM-2B
student: Multiple students: TinyLlama, GPT-2 variants, Pythia variants, TAID-LLM-1.5B (1.5B), TAID-VLM-2B (2B)
loss: KL divergence between temporally interpolated distribution (logit-level interpolation of detached student and teacher) and student distribution, with adaptive interpolation parameter t increasing from 0 to 1
task: LightEval benchmark suite (for TAID-LLM-1.5B), Open VLM Leaderboard (for TAID-VLM-2B), UltraChat 200k (instruction tuning), LAMBADA, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and various language modeling benchmarks
notes: TAID dynamically interpolates student and teacher logits via a time-dependent parameter t, creating an intermediate distribution that gradually shifts from student to teacher. Adaptive momentum-based update of t. Theoretical guarantee of non-collapse unlike self-distillation. Published at ICLR 2025.

teacher: GPT-5-Chat (closed-source, ranked 9th on Chatbot Text Arena leaderboard). Additional experiments use Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as teacher for cross-tokenizer distillation to Llama students.
student: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. All are instruction-tuned variants.
rationale: GPT-5-Chat chosen as a proprietary closed-source teacher to demonstrate black-box distillation where logits are inaccessible. Multiple student sizes (3B to 14B) used to evaluate scalability. Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct teacher used with Llama students to test cross-tokenizer incompatibility scenarios.
training_data: 200K samples from LMSYS-Chat-1M-Clean with corresponding GPT-5-Chat teacher responses. Test sets: 500 samples from LMSYS-Chat-1M-Clean, 500-sample Dolly subset, 252-sample SelfInst, 80-question Vicuna benchmark.
loss_details: Minimax objective: Generator maximizes D(G(x)) as reward via GRPO policy gradient (group size N=8, KL weight β=0.001). Discriminator minimizes Bradley-Terry loss: -log σ(D(y_t) - D(G(x))). Warmup stage: 1 epoch with cross-entropy loss for generator and Bradley-Terry loss for discriminator. GAD training: 2 epochs. Discriminator initialized from generator parameters with scalar prediction head. Learning rate 1e-6 for GAD with GPT-5 teacher (both warmup and GAD stages); 5e-6 warmup / 1e-6 GAD for Qwen2.5 teacher. Training temperature 0.8.
task: LMSYS-Chat test set (in-distribution), Dolly, SelfInst, Vicuna (out-of-distribution generalization). Evaluated via GPT-4o scores (student score / (student + reference score)). Human evaluation on LMSYS-Chat test set (win/tie/lose).
notes: GAD consistently outperforms SeqKD across all model sizes and datasets, with particularly strong gains on out-of-distribution benchmarks (Dolly, SelfInst, Vicuna) where SeqKD yields marginal or negative improvements. Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with GAD achieves 52.1 on LMSYS-Chat, surpassing the GPT-5-Chat teacher's 51.7. The on-policy discriminator avoids reward hacking that plagues off-policy approaches, remaining stable over thousands of training steps, while the off-policy variant exhibits reward hacking after ~300 steps with response lengths ballooning to 1300 tokens.

teacher: ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) serving three roles: Teacher, Referee, and Generator, accessed via OpenAI API. Exact parameter count not disclosed (proprietary).
student: LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-13B (pre-trained, open-source foundation models by Meta). Final models named Lion-7B and Lion-13B.
rationale: LLaMA was chosen as the open-source foundation model to distill proprietary ChatGPT knowledge into a compact model. The capacity ratio is not explicitly stated but involves distilling from a very large proprietary model (ChatGPT/GPT-3.5) to 7B and 13B parameter open-source models. The goal was to match ChatGPT capabilities while being significantly smaller and open-source.
training_data: Initial Train Pool and Cache Pool: 52K automatically generated instructions from Alpaca (generated from 175 manually selected seed instructions). 3 iterations of adversarial knowledge distillation with 6K newly generated instructions per iteration (1:1 ratio of hard to easy instructions). Total: 70K training data. No human annotation used.
loss_details: Standard autoregressive language modeling objective (next-token prediction) to align student responses with teacher responses during the imitation stage. No specific coefficients, temperatures, or mixture weights mentioned beyond the standard cross-entropy loss. The discrimination stage uses a threshold τ=1.0 on the score difference between teacher and student (scored on 1-10 scale by the referee/ChatGPT) to classify hard vs. easy instructions. ROUGE-L overlap threshold of 0.7 for deduplication of generated instructions.
task: Open-ended generation: Vicuna-Instructions (80 questions, 9 task categories, evaluated via GPT-4 as rater in two settings including balanced position calibration). Reasoning: AGIEval (8 English multiple-choice tasks, 2,546 samples) and BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) (23 multiple-choice tasks, 5,511 samples). All reasoning evaluated under zero-shot setting without CoT. Total of 40 sub-tasks across all benchmarks.
notes: Lion-13B achieved 98.38% of ChatGPT's capability on open-ended generation (Vicuna-Instructions), surpassing Vicuna-13B by ~6 points. The biggest improvements were on reasoning benchmarks: Lion-13B surpassed Vicuna-13B by 55.4% on BBH and 16.7% on AGIEval in zero-shot settings, with particularly large gains (>100%) on tasks involving data understanding, semantic understanding, logical/geometric reasoning, and position reasoning. However, Lion-13B still significantly lagged behind ChatGPT on reasoning, retaining only ~72.5% of ChatGPT's reasoning capability on AGIEval, confirming that while the adversarial framework improves over prior imitation methods, a substantial gap to the teacher remains on complex reasoning tasks.

teacher: GPT-4 (used indirectly via UltraChat dataset for SFT, and UltraFeedback dataset for preference data where GPT-4 provides preference rankings over responses from multiple models)
student: Mistral-7B (Mistral-7B-v0.1 base model)
rationale: The goal was to demonstrate that a smaller 7B model could achieve strong chat/instruction-following performance competitive with much larger aligned models (e.g., LLaMA-2-Chat-70B) through distilled direct preference optimization, using only distilled data from stronger teacher models without human annotation.
training_data: SFT phase: UltraChat dataset (~200k dialogues, filtered). Preference/DPO phase: UltraFeedback dataset (~64k prompts with responses from multiple models, scored by GPT-4; binarized by selecting highest and lowest scored responses as chosen/rejected pairs).
loss_details: Three-phase training: (1) Distilled SFT on UltraChat data using standard cross-entropy/NLL loss; (2) AI Feedback collection via GPT-4 scoring on UltraFeedback; (3) Distilled DPO (dDPO) using the standard DPO loss: L_DPO = -log σ(β(log π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x) - log π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x))) with β=0.1. The reference model π_ref is the SFT model from phase 1.
task: MT-Bench (multi-turn chat evaluation, GPT-4 as judge), AlpacaEval (single-turn instruction following, GPT-4 as judge), and Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA).
notes: Zephyr-7B-beta achieved the highest MT-Bench score (7.34) among models ≤13B at the time, outperforming LLaMA-2-Chat-70B on MT-Bench and approaching proprietary models. It showed particularly strong performance on chat/instruction-following benchmarks but had notable weaknesses on tasks requiring factual accuracy and safety, as it was not specifically trained with human safety annotations. The key finding was that distilled preference optimization from AI feedback alone could substitute for expensive RLHF with human annotators.

teacher: InternLM 2.5 7B-Chat, selected for strong performance and instruction-following ability with reliable adherence to Reason-then-Answer format in zero-shot prompting.
student: InternLM 2.5 1.8B-Chat and TinyLlama 1.1B-Instruct, chosen from different architecture families and sizes to validate cross-architecture distillation.
rationale: Cross-architecture distillation is the core goal; two students from different architecture families (InternLM vs TinyLlama) and sizes (1.8B vs 1.1B) were chosen to validate architecture-agnostic transfer from a 7B teacher. Capacity ratios are approximately 7B:1.8B (~3.9x) and 7B:1.1B (~6.4x).
training_data: Five multi-choice QA benchmark datasets: MedQA-USMLE (medical diagnostic reasoning), ARC-Challenge (general reasoning), StrategyQA (general reasoning), OpenBookQA (general reasoning), and GSM8K (mathematical problem-solving). Exact dataset sizes not specified. K=8 diverse reasoning traces sampled per example with temperature τ=0.8, filtered by rejection sampling discarding traces with ROUGE-L overlap > 0.80.
loss_details: ORPO objective: L_ORPO = L_SFT + λ * L_OR, where L_SFT = -log q_θ(y_P|x) (NLL on positive teacher trace) and L_OR = -log σ(log(odds q_θ(y_P|x) / odds q_θ(y_N|x))) (odds-ratio preference penalty). λ=1 for strong adaptation. Mixed-policy fraction ϕ=0.5 (equal mixing between base student model and latest checkpoint for negative trace generation). No temperature parameter on the loss itself; diversity sampling uses τ=0.8.
task: Five QA benchmarks: MedQA-USMLE, ARC-Challenge, StrategyQA, OpenBookQA, GSM8K. Evaluation metric is accuracy (%).
notes: Mixed-Policy ORPO-Distill consistently achieves the best results across all five datasets and both student models, with the largest gains on ARC-Challenge (e.g., +17.17% absolute over diverse CoT fine-tuning for InternLM 2.5 1.8B-Chat) and MedQA (+9.87% for the same student). Purely on-policy updates degraded performance compared to off-policy, attributed to narrowing negative trace diversity; mixed-policy mitigates this by anchoring to the initial student distribution. The method does not yet extend to open-ended generation tasks, as it relies on ground-truth labels for classifying traces as positive/negative.

teacher: Privileged student: a frozen copy of the student model conditioned on the ground-truth expert solution (not a separate larger teacher model). A negative reference model (also a frozen copy) conditioned only on isolated intermediate results is used for the contrastive term.
student: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (trained on e1-verifiable) and Qwen3-8B (think) (trained on e1-proof)
rationale: DAIL is designed for settings where no stronger teacher exists and standard RLVR fails because the student cannot sample correct solutions. The privileged student and negative reference share the same architecture and weights as the student, avoiding the need for a larger teacher. The method targets problems the student model itself cannot solve even with 32 attempts.
training_data: e1-verifiable: 417 historical AIME problems (1985-2023) with community-generated solutions from AoPS Wiki, filtered to problems unsolved by Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in 32 attempts. e1-proof: 669 non-verifiable Olympiad proof problems from IMO and regional contests with expert solutions authored by a current IMO coach (Evan Chen). Both datasets contain fewer than 1000 examples.
loss_details: Contrastive KL-divergence objective: L(theta) = sum over tokens t of [ DKL(M_theta(.|x, r<t) || M_PS(.|r<t)) - gamma * DKL(M_theta(.|x, r<t) || M_NR(.|r<t)) ], where M_PS is the privileged student, M_NR is the negative reference model, and 0 <= gamma <= 1 is a hyperparameter. The first term distills from the privileged student; the second term penalizes tokens with high probability under the negative reference to suppress rationalization shortcuts.
task: AIME 2024/2025, BeyondAIME (100 hard AIME-style problems), IMO-AnswerBench (400 Olympiad-level problems), and GPQA-Diamond (198 graduate-level science questions) as out-of-domain generalization. Evaluated using unbiased pass@k metric with varying k.
granularity: Token-level (token-level KL divergence computed at each position in the reasoning trace)
notes: DAIL achieves 10-25% pass@k gains on challenging math benchmarks using fewer than 1000 expert solutions, while also improving reasoning efficiency by 2-4x fewer tokens. Notably, it enables a 15% gain for Qwen3 (think) on IMO-AnswerBench and generalizes out-of-domain to GPQA-Diamond. The method is orders of magnitude more training-efficient than GRPO (0.1 vs 277.6 H100 hours per epoch on e1-verifiable), and uniquely enables learning from non-verifiable proof problems where standard RLVR cannot provide any training signal.

teacher: No external teacher. The model serves as its own opponent via self-play: the previous iteration's model (pθt) generates synthetic responses that the current iteration's model (pθt+1) learns to distinguish from human-annotated responses.
student: zephyr-7b-sft-full (Mistral-7B fine-tuned on Ultrachat200k SFT dataset by HuggingFace), 7B parameters.
rationale: The goal is to improve a weak SFT model without additional human-annotated data or stronger external models. No capacity ratio applies as teacher and student are the same model across iterations.
training_data: 50k prompts randomly sampled from Ultrachat200k (a 200k high-quality subset of UltraChat ~1.4M dialogues). Only the first round of multi-round conversations is used. At iteration 0: 50k synthetic pairs; at iterations 1-3: 100k synthetic pairs (50k from previous iteration + 50k newly generated). For SPIN+DPO experiment, an additional 62k preference data from UltraFeedback Binarized dataset was used.
loss_details: Self-play objective resembling DPO-style preference optimization: the model learns to prefer human-annotated responses over self-generated responses from the previous iteration. β=0.1 for iterations 0-2, increased to β=5.0 at iteration 3 (final iteration near convergence). Max sequence length 2048 tokens. Optimizer: RMSProp with no weight decay, global batch size 64, 10% warmup steps, bfloat16 precision. Peak learning rate 5e-7 for iterations 0-1, decayed to 1e-7 for iterations 2-3. 2 epochs per iteration.
task: HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard (Arc 25-shot, TruthfulQA 0-shot, Winogrande 5-shot, GSM8k 5-shot, HellaSwag 10-shot, MMLU 5-shot), MT-Bench, Big-Bench-Hard (Causal Judgment, Sports Understanding, Formal Fallacies), OpenBookQA.
notes: SPIN improved the base zephyr-7b-sft-full from 58.14 to 63.16 average on Open LLM Leaderboard and from 5.94 to 6.78 on MT-Bench over 4 iterations, with the largest gains on GSM8k (+12.21 absolute) and TruthfulQA (+11.17 absolute). At iteration 0, SPIN already matched DPO trained with 62k additional GPT-4 preference data, and surpassed it from iteration 1 onward. Diminishing returns were observed across iterations (improvements of +2.66, +1.32, +0.85, +0.19), and MMLU showed slight degradation, suggesting the method is bounded by the quality ceiling of the original human-annotated SFT data.

teacher: Same model as student (self-distillation): Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B-Instruct. The teacher policy is the initial (frozen) policy conditioned on privileged information (problem + ground-truth CoT solution).
student: Same model as teacher: Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B-Instruct. The student policy is conditioned only on the problem. Trained with LoRA (rank=64, alpha=128) on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down projection modules.
rationale: The key insight is that a single model can serve as both teacher and student by conditioning on different contexts—the teacher sees privileged ground-truth solutions while the student sees only the problem. This eliminates the need for a separate larger teacher model. The paper tests across 1.7B, 4B, and 8B scales to study the effect of model capacity on self-distillation effectiveness.
training_data: Mathematical reasoning subset of OpenThoughts (Guha et al., 2025), up to 30K problem-solution pairs with chain-of-thought reasoning.
loss_details: Per-token divergence minimization using JSD_β=0.5 (generalized Jensen-Shannon Divergence with β=0.5) between teacher and student next-token distributions over the full vocabulary, averaged over token positions in the student's on-policy rollout. Learning rate 2e-5 or 2e-4 (2e-4 for lower generation lengths like 1024). Full-vocabulary logit distillation used by default. Teacher policy is frozen to the initial policy (not updated during training). Gradients flow only through student logits.
task: Competition-level mathematical reasoning: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, HMMT 2025, AMO-Bench. Evaluated using average@16 with temperature 1.0 and 38k generation length.
notes: OPSD matches or exceeds GRPO at 4B and 8B scales while using only 1 rollout per problem vs. GRPO's 8, achieving 8-12× token efficiency. The biggest improvements appear on HMMT25 (e.g., Qwen3-4B: 45.2 vs. 42.7 for GRPO) and AMO-Bench at 4B scale. However, OPSD underperforms at 1.7B scale (e.g., drops on HMMT25 from 26.7 GRPO to 25.0), indicating that sufficient model capacity is necessary for effective self-distillation. Full-vocabulary logit distillation outperforms sampled-token distillation (84.1% vs 82.1% on AIME25 pass@8).

teacher: Same model as student (self-distillation): Qwen3-8B or Qwen3-14B conditioned on a conciseness instruction c. Teacher weights periodically synchronized with student every M=50 steps. No external or larger teacher model used.
student: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B (same model as teacher but without conciseness instruction).
rationale: Self-distillation approach where teacher and student share the same parameters but differ in conditioning context. The teacher receives a conciseness instruction prepended to the input, enabling the model to distill its own concise behavior back into itself without needing a separate larger model. No capacity ratio applies since teacher=student.
training_data: DAPO-Math-17k (~17,000 competition-level math problems), split 80/20 into ~13,600 training prompts and ~3,400 validation prompts with a fixed seed.
loss_details: Per-token reverse KL divergence: DKL(π_student ∥ π_teacher) summed over all token positions in student-generated rollouts, normalized by sequence length. No temperature parameter mentioned (implicit τ=1.0). No mixture with NLL or other losses. No correctness filtering applied. AdamW optimizer with constant learning rate 1e-6, weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping max norm 1.0, global batch size 32, micro-batch size 2 per GPU, 1 epoch, bfloat16 precision.
task: MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025 (math reasoning benchmarks). Also evaluated on MMLU for general capability preservation. Evaluation uses mean@8 accuracy (8 samples per problem, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, max 30K generation tokens).
notes: OPSDC achieves the biggest improvements on MATH-500: +16.1 points accuracy with 57% token reduction for Qwen3-14B (70.0%→86.1%) and +8.9 points with 59% reduction for Qwen3-8B. On AIME 2024, Qwen3-14B gains +10.5 points with 41% compression. However, on the harder AIME 2025, accuracy drops slightly (-5.4 points for 14B) despite 35% compression, and extended training to step 200 further degrades AIME performance while maintaining MATH-500 accuracy, suggesting compression on harder benchmarks is less sustainable. Forward KL was shown to cause progressive accuracy collapse with saw-tooth instability at teacher refresh boundaries.

teacher: Qwen3-4B-Base (tutor role: same model conditioned on document d and question q). Questions pre-generated by Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct from Nemotron-CC-Math corpus.
student: Qwen3-4B-Base (student role: same model conditioned on question q alone, no document access). Tutor and student share identical weights.
rationale: Self-distillation setting: the same model serves as both tutor and student, differing only in input context (privileged document access vs. no document). The asymmetry in input context creates the imbalance that standard distillation obtains from a larger teacher, enabling self-improvement without external oracles. No capacity ratio since same model.
training_data: 551 training questions and 50 held-out evaluation questions generated by prompting Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on documents from the Nemotron-CC-Math corpus (one question per document). Questions filtered by requiring ≥5/8 tutor consensus, parsable \boxed{} answer, and document-leakage guardrails.
loss_details: Total loss: L(θ) = λ_off * L_off + λ_on * L_on. Canonical GATES: λ_off=1.0, λ_on=0.1, λ_cons=0.0, λ_KL=0.02. L_off is off-policy trajectory distillation (token-level cross-entropy on tutor rollout tokens, evaluated under student prompt without document). L_on is on-policy advantage-weighted loss using token-level advantage A_t = log π_θ(y_t|y_{<t},d,q) - log π_θ(y_t|y_{<t},q) clipped to [-a, a]. Consensus gate: question skipped (zero loss) if fewer than 4/8 tutor rollouts agree; rollout-level gate retains only trajectories matching consensus answer. KL regularization toward frozen reference policy. All losses computed on completion tokens only (prompt tokens masked), normalized by total included completion tokens.
task: In-domain: held-out asymmetric evaluation (50 questions, greedy decoding). Out-of-domain: four public document-free math benchmarks — MATH, AMC, Minerva, OlympiadBench — evaluated with maj@8 (majority voting over 8 samples).
notes: GATES improved held-out in-domain student accuracy from 46.0% to 62.0% and average maj@8 on public math benchmarks from 20.2% to 35.4%. The consensus gate is the critical mechanism: removing it alone (−Gate) drops performance to match unfiltered Tutor-Trajectory SFT (54% in-domain, 31.1% benchmark avg). Answer-only SFT catastrophically degraded accuracy to 10–12%, and Outcome RL provided no meaningful improvement over the pretrained base, confirming that dense trajectory-level distillation with reliability filtering is essential.

teacher: Self-teacher: the same model (e.g., Qwen3-8B or Olmo3-7B-Instruct) conditioned on rich feedback f, i.e., πθ(·|x, f, y<t). No external teacher is used. A teacher-EMA (exponential moving average) is also employed with update rates of 0.05 (without feedback) or 0.01 (with feedback/TTT).
student: Qwen3-8B (Qwen/Qwen3-8B) and Olmo3-7B-Instruct (allenai/Olmo3-7B-Instruct), both with thinking disabled (Thinking=False).
rationale: The same model serves as both student and teacher (self-distillation), leveraging the model's in-context learning ability to retrospectively identify mistakes when conditioned on feedback. No capacity ratio applies since teacher and student are the same model. SDPO's gains grow with model scale, suggesting self-teaching emerges as models become stronger in-context learners.
training_data: Section 3 (without rich feedback): Scientific reasoning tasks (Chemistry, Physics, Biology, Materials) and Tool Use benchmarks. Section 4 (with rich feedback): LiveCodeBench v6 (LCBv6), 131 competitive programming questions released Feb–May 2025, with LeetCode-style feedback (runtime errors, failed unit tests). Section 5 (TTT): Very difficult LCBv6 questions with pass@64 < 0.03. Exact dataset sizes not explicitly stated.
loss_details: KL-divergence distillation loss: L_SDPO(θ) = Σ_t KL(πθ(·|x, y<t) ∥ stopgrad(πθ(·|x, f, y<t))). stopgrad blocks gradients through the teacher. Section 3 (without feedback): Top-K=100 distillation, Jensen–Shannon divergence, teacher-EMA update rate=0.05, rollout importance sampling clip=2. Section 4 (with feedback): Top-K=20, Reverse-KL divergence, teacher-EMA update rate=0.01, rollout importance sampling clip=2. Section 5 (TTT): Top-K=20, Reverse-KL, clip advantages=5.0, teacher-EMA update rate=0.01, rollout importance sampling clip=2. No explicit temperature parameter mentioned for distillation.
task: Section 3: Chemistry, Physics, Biology, Materials Science (scientific reasoning MCQ), and Tool Use — evaluated with avg@16. Section 4: LiveCodeBench v6 (LCBv6) competitive programming — 131 problems, accuracy metric. Section 5: Test-Time Self-Distillation on hard LCBv6 questions (pass@64 < 0.03), measuring discovery probability with 3× fewer attempts.
notes: SDPO showed the biggest improvements on Chemistry (80.9% vs 74.5% for Qwen3-8B; 80.0% vs 56.7% for Olmo3-7B-Instruct at 5h) and on LiveCodeBench v6 (48.8% vs 41.2% over GRPO, achieving GRPO's final accuracy in 4× fewer generations). SDPO consistently produced 3× shorter responses than GRPO while achieving higher accuracy, avoiding circular reasoning patterns. A key limitation is that SDPO's performance depends on the model's in-context learning ability, and it can underperform GRPO on weaker models with poor in-context learning capabilities.

teacher: Same pretrained checkpoint as student, frozen during training. Experiments use Llama-3.1-8B (initialized from Llama-3.1-8B with Magpie data) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. Teacher uses argmax ('hard teacher') readout.
student: Llama-3.1-8B-Magpie (8B params) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (4B params). Both initialized from the same pretrained checkpoint as their respective teacher (θT0 = θS0). All student parameters are trainable.
rationale: Self-distillation is chosen so that at training step 0 with k=1, the student and teacher predictions are identical and the loss is 0, ensuring a well-behaved initial loss landscape. No capacity ratio between teacher and student since they share the same architecture and initialization.
training_data: Primary: MetaMathQA (~50M tokens under Llama 3 tokenizer, avg ~220 tokens/sample, truncated to 160 tokens). Ablations use Magpie datasets (sequence length 1024). Models see ~500M supervised tokens over ~100k training iterations (~35 epochs of MetaMathQA for L3.1-8B-Magpie model).
loss_details: Online KL divergence loss: L_MTP = -P_θT(y'|x_{1:i}) log P_θS(y'|x_{1:i}), where y' = argmax(ℓ_{i:i+k}) is the student's deterministic rollout and teacher scores it via chain rule of probability. 'Hard teacher' variant used (argmax readout for teacher, reducing teacher distribution to delta/zero-entropy). No auxiliary NTP loss on prefix tokens. No temperature parameter mentioned. No mixture weights. Entropy term of KL omitted as constant w.r.t. student parameters.
task: GSM8K (CoT Fewshot, flexible-extract accuracy), AIME25 (exact-match), GPQA, BBH (CoT Fewshot, exact-match), IFEval (Prompt-level exact-match), CNN DailyMail (ROUGE-L).
notes: The method achieves >3× acceleration on GSM8K with <5% accuracy drop (L3.1-8B-Magpie) using confidence-adaptive decoding at 90% threshold; Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507 achieves 3× at ~7% accuracy drop. Strongest results and largest acceleration factors are on GSM8K and BBH (structured reasoning tasks), while more open-ended generative tasks like CNN DailyMail yield lower acceleration factors across all adaptive decoding configurations, suggesting the method works best where low-entropy, predictable token sequences dominate.

teacher: Context-conditioned teacher model; configurations include: (1) frozen larger model (e.g., Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) for teacher-student distillation, (2) same-weight model with context access for self-distillation. Teacher receives concatenated [context c; input x; response y] to compute target probabilities.
student: Same-family models of equal or smaller size: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and smaller Qwen3 models (for cross-size distillation). Student generates responses without context c and is updated via gradient descent.
rationale: On-policy sampling with reverse KL addresses exposure bias and mode-covering issues of off-policy forward KL context distillation. Cross-size distillation is explored (e.g., Qwen3-8B teacher to smaller Qwen3 students) because directly injecting teacher-generated experiential knowledge into smaller model contexts degrades performance, motivating parameter internalization.
training_data: Training data D consists of (input x, context c) pairs across: (1) mathematical reasoning datasets for experiential knowledge distillation, (2) text-based game environments (Frozen Lake, Sokoban), (3) domain-specific tasks with optimized system prompts (medical QA, safety classification). Exact dataset sizes not specified.
loss_details: Reverse KL divergence minimized on-policy: L(theta) = E_{(x,c)~D, y~pi_theta(.|x)} [ (1/|y|) * sum_{t=1}^{|y|} DKL(pi_theta(.|x,y<t) || pi_teacher(.|c,x,y<t)) ], where token-level KL is computed as sum over top-k student-predicted tokens: sum_{y_t in V_top-k} pi_theta(y_t|x,y<t) * (log pi_theta(y_t|x,y<t) - log pi_teacher(y_t|c,x,y<t)).
task: Mathematical reasoning (math validation dataset), text-based games (Frozen Lake, Sokoban), domain-specific tasks (medical QA, safety classification), and out-of-distribution evaluation on IF-Eval benchmark.
notes: OPCD consistently outperforms off-policy context distillation baselines across all tasks, achieving higher in-distribution accuracy while mitigating catastrophic forgetting on OOD tasks (approximately 2% higher IF-Eval scores on Frozen Lake, ~4 points better OOD preservation on safety-to-medical transfer). Teacher-student distillation substantially outperforms self-distillation (e.g., 53.9% vs 18.8% on Sokoban), attributed to training instability from using a continuously evolving model as teacher. Cross-size distillation is effective: smaller students improve via OPCD from larger teacher experiential knowledge, whereas directly injecting that knowledge into smaller model contexts degrades performance.

teacher: The same model πθ augmented with experiential knowledge in context serves as the teacher (πteacher = πθ, frozen). Models used: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B (thinking), and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (non-thinking). The teacher is the knowledge-conditioned version of the current policy model, not a separate larger model.
student: The same model πθ without experiential knowledge context serves as the student. Models: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B (thinking), Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (non-thinking). The extraction model πextract is also set to πθ.
rationale: The teacher and student are the same model (self-play/self-distillation), differing only in whether experiential knowledge is provided in context. This enables reward-free on-policy learning without requiring a separate larger teacher. Multiple model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) and both thinking/non-thinking variants are tested to demonstrate generality. An ablation shows on-policy knowledge from the model's own trajectories benefits more than off-policy knowledge from a larger model (Qwen3-4B).
training_data: Two text-based game environments from TextArena: Frozen Lake (3×3 grid, 2 holes) and Sokoban (6×6 grid, 1 box). No explicit rules provided. For extraction: n=25 or n=50 trajectories for structured format, n=15 for unstructured format, with K=10 accumulation repetitions. For consolidation: 1280 or 6400 trajectory samples per training round (20 or 100 steps × 64 game samples per step). Each interaction spans up to 5 turns with max 1024 tokens per turn. Evaluation on held-out test split of 128 game maps averaged over 10 random seeds. OOD evaluation on IF-Eval.
loss_details: Reverse KL divergence (on-policy context distillation). Loss: L(θ) = (1/|y|) Σ_{t=1}^{|y|} D_KL(πθ(·|x,y<t) ∥ πteacher(·|e,x,y<t)), where y ~ πθ(·|x) is sampled on-policy from the student. The KL is approximated using top-k=256 tokens from the student's predicted probability. No temperature parameter explicitly mentioned. No mixture with NLL. No reward model or verifiable reward used.
task: Text-based game environments: Frozen Lake (grid navigation avoiding holes) and Sokoban (spatial reasoning puzzle). Metrics: pass rate on held-out 128 game maps (averaged over 10 seeds), normalized response length (token efficiency), and out-of-distribution performance on IF-Eval (prompt-level strict accuracy).
notes: OEL achieves consistent improvements over successive iterations on both Frozen Lake and Sokoban, with Qwen3-1.7B reaching ~50% pass rate from near 0% on Frozen Lake across multiple rounds. The method simultaneously improves token efficiency, reducing response length to ~70% by the third iteration. On-policy context distillation preserves out-of-distribution IF-Eval performance (~67% accuracy maintained) while off-policy distillation degrades it. Key findings: extracted experiential knowledge is significantly more effective than raw trajectories, and on-policy consistency is critical—on-policy knowledge from the model's own trajectories outperforms off-policy knowledge from a larger Qwen3-4B model.

teacher: DeepSeek-R1 (671B parameters, MoE architecture with 37B activated parameters). The full reinforcement learning-trained reasoning model serves as the teacher.
student: Multiple student models: Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen2.5-32B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. These are fine-tuned from their base/instruct checkpoints.
rationale: The authors chose to distill from DeepSeek-R1 to smaller dense models to demonstrate that the reasoning capabilities discovered via large-scale RL can be transferred to much smaller models more efficiently than applying RL directly to small models. The capacity ratio ranges from ~447x (671B→1.5B) to ~9.6x (671B→70B).
training_data: 800,000 samples curated from DeepSeek-R1's generated outputs, covering a mix of reasoning-intensive domains. The distillation data consists of long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces generated by DeepSeek-R1. Exact dataset composition details beyond the 800k sample count are not fully specified.
loss_details: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the teacher-generated reasoning traces using standard next-token prediction (NLL/cross-entropy loss). No KL divergence or logit-matching losses are mentioned — this is a black-box distillation approach using only the teacher's output sequences. Specific temperatures or mixture weights are 未明确.
task: AIME 2024 (math competition), MATH-500, GPQA Diamond (graduate-level science QA), LiveCodeBench (code generation), Codeforces (competitive programming), SWE-Bench Verified (software engineering). Also evaluated on general benchmarks: MMLU, MMLU-Redux, MMLU-Pro, IF-Eval, C-Eval, CLUEWSP.
notes: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B achieved 72.6% on AIME 2024 pass@1 and 94.3% on MATH-500, outperforming OpenAI's o1-mini on several reasoning benchmarks. The distilled models showed the biggest improvements on math and code reasoning tasks compared to their base models. Notably, distillation from DeepSeek-R1 to small models significantly outperformed applying RL directly to those small models, suggesting that reasoning patterns are more effectively transferred via distillation than discovered independently through RL at small scale. Performance on general/non-reasoning benchmarks showed less dramatic gains or slight regressions.

teacher: DeepSeek-R1 (used to generate reasoning paths in the OpenR1-Math dataset)
student: Qwen2.5-Math-7B (RL-only setting, yielding Qwen2.5-Math-7B-RLKD-Zero) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (SFT-distilled 7B model, further trained with RLKD)
rationale: Demonstrates that RL-based distillation of implicit multi-branch reasoning structure can outperform SFT-RL pipelines even with drastically less data (0.1%); 7B student models are used as resource-constrained alternatives to the much larger DeepSeek-R1 teacher
training_data: OpenR1-Math (with DeepSeek-R1-generated reasoning paths); approximately 0.1% of the data used in the SFT-RL pipeline for the RL-only setting; a 3.2K subset selected via embedding similarity for the SFT vs RL distillation comparison experiment
loss_details: GRPO (Group-based Relative Policy Optimization) combined with a weighted sum of the Generative Structure Reward Model (GSRM) reward and a task-specific outcome reward (e.g., math accuracy). GSRM is a two-stage reward: first converts reasoning paths into meta-reasoning-solving step sequences via a generative model, then scores structural alignment between student and teacher step sequences using a rule-based structured reward mechanism.
task: AIME24 (math reasoning), MATH-500 (math reasoning), and GPQA-Diamond (graduate-level Q&A); evaluated with pass@1 (averaged over m=64 for AIME, m=8 for GPQA, m=4 for MATH500) and pass@k (k>1) to assess diverse path exploration
notes: RLKD with only 0.1% of training data under an RL-only regime surpasses the full SFT-RL pipeline of Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, demonstrating that structural reasoning alignment is more data-efficient than token-level imitation. When applied on top of the already SFT-distilled DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, RLKD yields further gains where standard PPO and GRPO baselines show negligible improvement, particularly on pass@k (k>1) metrics that measure the model's ability to explore multiple diverse reasoning paths. This confirms that RLKD distills the implicit multi-branch reasoning structure rather than merely memorizing the teacher's output sequences.

teacher: Qwen3-8B (for logic reasoning) and Qwen3-8B/Qwen3-32B (for complex math reasoning)
student: Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B (for logic reasoning); Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base (for complex math reasoning), ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters
rationale: Teacher-student pairs chosen to evaluate distillation across varying capacity ratios (0.6B/1.7B vs 8B, and 1.7B/8B vs 8B/32B), motivated by the high inference cost of large RL-trained reasoning models and the need to compress them into smaller deployable students
training_data: K&K Logistics dataset for logic reasoning; Skywork-OR1 training set (105K samples) for complex math reasoning
loss_details: Trust Region Ratio Distillation (TRRD): replaces the standard teacher-student KL regularizer with a PPO/GRPO-style clipped importance-ratio objective anchored to a teacher-old-policy mixture distribution. The TRRD ratio is computed from a mixture anchor (pi_old^alpha * pi_teacher^(1-alpha)), clipped within [1-epsilon, 1+epsilon], and weighted by group-relative advantages. The full RLAD objective combines the TRRD clipped surrogate loss with a KL regularization term against a reference policy (beta * KL(pi_student || pi_ref))
task: Logic reasoning: K&K Logistics dataset (PPL2-PPL8 difficulty subsets) with 2K and 8K context lengths. Math reasoning: AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, AMC24, MATH500 evaluated with Pass@1 and Pass@32 metrics at 8K-30K response budgets
notes: RLAD achieves substantial improvements over vanilla GRPO and KDRL baselines, with the largest gains on the hardest benchmarks (e.g., PPL7/PPL8 in logic, AIME24/25 Pass@32 in math), while simpler benchmarks like MATH500 show smaller improvements suggesting capacity saturation. Compared to KDRL, RLAD exhibits more stable training dynamics with fewer validation oscillations and stronger Pass@1 gains, indicating a better balance between teacher imitation and reward-driven policy improvement. The selective imitation mechanism of TRRD enables advantage-aware distillation that avoids uniformly pushing the student toward the teacher in regions where teacher behavior conflicts with high-reward trajectories.

teacher: Synthetic teacher distribution constructed from a DPO model and a reverse DPO model (both trained from the same initial instruct models: Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The teacher logit is an adaptive extrapolation: z_t* = z_t^dpo + α_t(z_t^dpo - z_t^{dpo-}). Not a separate larger teacher model.
student: Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as primary models; also evaluated on Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3-8B for larger-scale experiments. For TL;DR experiments, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Base with SFT.
rationale: The method is not traditional teacher-student distillation with a capacity gap. Instead, the 'teacher' is a synthetic distribution derived from contrastive DPO models (normal + reverse DPO) of the same size as the student, constructed to be stronger than either individual model via logit extrapolation. No capacity ratio applies.
training_data: UltraFeedback (~63K prompts with preference-annotated response pairs). For on-policy AlignDistil, only prompts are used; for off-policy AlignDistil, prompts and chosen responses are used. Also evaluated on TL;DR (SFT and preference datasets). Larger model experiments use UltraChat-200k for Qwen2.5-7B SFT.
loss_details: Token-level KL divergence loss: L = (1/|B|) * Σ (β_t/|y|) * Σ_t D_KL(π_θ(·|y<t,x) || π*(·|y<t,x)), where π* is softmax over z_t* = z_t^dpo + α_t(z_t^dpo - z_t^{dpo-}). α_t = D_TVD(t) * r + ε, where ε=0.001, r is a hyperparameter (r=20 for Qwen2-1.5B on-policy, r=15 for Qwen2.5-1.5B on-policy, r=10 for Qwen2-1.5B off-policy, r=15 for Qwen2.5-1.5B off-policy, r=1 off-policy and r=2 on-policy for TL;DR). β_t = β_0/α_t is adaptive per token. DPO models trained with β_0=0.1.
task: AlpacaEval 2.0 (LC WR and WR), MT-Bench (1st Turn, 2nd Turn, Avg. scores), Arena-Hard (WR and SC WR), and TL;DR summarization (win rate vs SFT, average reward). Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct used as evaluator.
notes: AlignDistil showed the largest improvements on AlpacaEval 2.0 and Arena-Hard, with on-policy achieving 12.93% LC WR vs 8.92% for the best baseline (RTO) on Qwen2-1.5B, and 24.1% WR on Arena-Hard vs 18.2% for RTO on Qwen2.5-1.5B. It demonstrated >2× faster convergence than token-level scalar reward methods due to distributional (full KL) optimization rather than scalar rewards. The method is limited to small models (~1.5B primarily) due to resource constraints, and the off-policy variant sometimes matches or exceeds on-policy performance (e.g., on Qwen2.5-1.5B), suggesting efficient training without online sampling is viable.

teacher: DeepSeek-R1 (off-policy reasoning traces from OpenR1-Math-220k dataset). πϕ is set to 1 in practice for computational efficiency, avoiding tokenization mismatch between teacher and student models.
student: Qwen2.5-Math-7B (default), also extended to Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Instruct-7B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
rationale: DeepSeek-R1 serves as a stronger reasoning model providing off-policy guidance to transcend the on-policy RL limitation where models can only learn from their own generations. Weak models like LLaMA-3.1-8B are used to demonstrate LUFFY succeeds where on-policy RL completely fails due to insufficient base model capability.
training_data: Subset of OpenR1-Math-220k (prompts from NuminaMath 1.5, off-policy traces from DeepSeek-R1). Default subset of 94k prompts filtered to 45k prompts after removing generations >8192 tokens and those verified wrong by Math-Verify. For LLaMA-3.1-8B: Easy subset (R1 solutions <2k tokens, 7.3k prompts) and Hard subset (R1 solutions <4k tokens, 25.4k prompts).
loss_details: Mixed-Policy GRPO (Eq. 5/6): combines off-policy objective with policy shaping f(r̂) = r̂/(r̂+γ) where γ=0.1, and on-policy clipped GRPO objective. Advantage computed over union of on-policy and off-policy rewards (Eq. 4). β=0 (no KL loss), entropy loss coefficient=0.01. Length normalization and standard error normalization removed (following Dr.GRPO). Clip operation omitted for off-policy rollouts. πϕ=1 for off-policy importance sampling. 1 off-policy + 7 on-policy rollouts per prompt (8 total). Binary verifiable reward (correct=1, incorrect=0) via Math-Verify.
task: In-distribution: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC (avg@32), MATH-500, Minerva, OlympiadBench (pass@1). Out-of-distribution: ARC-c, GPQA-diamond, MMLU-Pro. Generation temperature=0.6 for testing, temperature=1.0 for rollout generation.
notes: LUFFY achieves +6.4 average gain over prior RLVR methods across six math benchmarks and +6.2 on OOD tasks with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, establishing new SOTA for RLVR. Most critically, LUFFY successfully trains LLaMA-3.1-8B on hard datasets where on-policy RL completely fails (training rewards collapse to zero), demonstrating it transcends base model capacity limitations. Compared to SFT+RL, LUFFY uses only 59% GPU hours and less off-policy data while achieving +1.9 in-distribution and +16.1 OOD improvements, as SFT causes rigid imitation and excessive generation lengths that inflate RL rollout costs.

teacher: o1-mini and gpt-4o-mini (for hierarchical thought template extraction in Stage 1); o1-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini (for cross-model correction traces in Stage 2); o1-preview (as inspector LLM for quality verification)
student: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeekMath-7B-Instruct (all 7B/8B scale)
rationale: Smaller models (7B/8B) struggle with complex mathematical reasoning and cannot independently identify and correct reasoning errors. SOTA large teacher models (o1-mini, GPT-4o) provide hierarchical thought templates and cross-model correction traces to break the reasoning bottleneck of smaller student models. Capacity ratio is roughly 7B student vs. frontier closed-source teacher models.
training_data: Stage 1 (HSFT): 100k samples constructed from MATH training set (7,500 problems), GSM8K training set (7,473 problems), 670 translated GaoKao Bench problems, plus samples from NuminaMath and MetaMath, with hierarchical thought templates generated by o1-mini/gpt-4o-mini. Stage 2 (Cross-model DPO): 10k pair-wise preference samples (from 20k incorrect reasoning results collected from three different SFT models), consisting of chosen teacher corrections and rejected student self-corrections.
loss_details: Stage 1: Standard SFT loss (maximize log-likelihood of hierarchical thought template responses). Stage 2: Cross-model collaborative DPO loss: L_Cross-DPO(θ) = -E[log σ(β log(π_θ(a+,c+|x;s_{1~k-1})/π_ref(a+,c+|x;s_{1~k-1})) - β log(π_θ(a-,c-|x;s_{1~k-1})/π_ref(a-,c-|x;s_{1~k-1})))], where (a+,c+) is teacher's correction trace (chosen) and (a-,c-) is student's self-correction trace (rejected), applied at the first error step k. β hyperparameter controls distance from reference model (exact value not specified).
task: MATH (5,000 test problems, competition-level mathematics) and GSM8K (1,319 test problems, grade school math). Chain-of-thought reasoning accuracy evaluated using lm-evaluation-harness framework.
notes: SuperCorrect-Qwen-7B achieved 70.2% on MATH (+15.1% over Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct) and 89.5% on GSM8K (+6.3%), setting new SOTA among 7B models. The biggest gains came from the cross-model DPO stage, which added +7.1% on MATH over HSFT alone (vs. only +0.7% from Reflexion), demonstrating that teacher-guided error correction is far more effective than self-correction. The method also uniquely improved self-correction ability by 5-6% accuracy post-correction, while other LLMs showed no improvement or even degraded performance during self-correction attempts.

teacher: Skywork-OR1-Math-7B (for main experiments with 1.5B student); Qwen2.5-7B-GRPO (a GRPO-trained Qwen2.5-7B, for R1-Zero-like experiments with 3B student)
student: DeepScaleR-1.5B-8K (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B trained on DeepScaleR dataset under 8K context, main experiments); Qwen2.5-3B (R1-Zero-like experiments)
rationale: Teacher-student capacity ratio of approximately 4.7x (7B teacher to 1.5B student) in main experiments and approximately 2.3x (7B to 3B) in zero-RL experiments. KD alone generalizes poorly out-of-domain while RL alone suffers from low sample efficiency; combining them leverages teacher supervision for efficient learning and self-exploration for better generalization.
training_data: Skywork-OR1-RL-Data corpus with difficulty-controlled sampling; preprocessed to 61K math problems after filtering by solvability (constraining unsolved examples to 10%) and prompt length (max 1024 tokens). 16 rollouts per prompt with 20K context length.
loss_details: Joint loss: JKDRL(theta) = JGRPO(theta) - beta * Dk2_KL(pi_theta || pi_T), where JGRPO is the on-policy GRPO objective with token-level loss and no KL constraint, and Dk2_KL is the k2 KL approximation (0.5 * R_i,t(theta)^2) of the reverse KL divergence between student and teacher. Fixed beta=2e-3 for KDRL; for KDRL-Annealing, beta_init=5e-3, delta=5e-5, beta_min=1e-3. Response-level KL masking applied to select hard samples for KD. Reward is binary rule-based: r = r_format * r_acc.
task: Mathematical reasoning benchmarks: MATH500, MinervaMath, OlympiadBench (Pass@1), and competition-level datasets AIME24, AIME25, AMC23 (Avg@16 over 16 decoding runs)
notes: KDRL outperforms GRPO by 2.6% and SFT by 5.7% on average across benchmarks, and also surpasses on-policy KD-RKL by 1.1%, demonstrating that jointly optimizing distillation and RL is more effective than either alone or sequential application. The k2 KL estimator was found superior to k3 and Top-K alternatives due to its unbiased gradient property, and KDRL-Annealing (which gradually reduces the KD coefficient) achieved the best overall results (57.2% average) while maintaining favorable reasoning token efficiency compared to pure RL approaches that exhibit unconstrained length growth.

teacher: Qwen3-VL-32B (used for both hint generation and on-policy distillation)
student: Qwen3-VL-2B (instruction-tuned variant)
rationale: 16x capacity ratio (32B teacher vs 2B student). The large teacher provides dense token-level guidance and reasoning hints to the smaller student, which is trained under a low-resource regime to study reasoning emergence and OOD generalization.
training_data: 600 MRI image-question pairs randomly sampled from the OmniMedVQA benchmark training split (single-source domain generalization setting). Evaluation on 2,400 test instances (300 per modality × 8 modalities).
